ext.title: Shortest Path Algorithms for Social Network Strengths
ext.year: Not stated in extracted text (data runs to Feb 2010; references include a 2010 item)
ext.venue: Not visible in extracted text (LNCS-style layout per metadata hint; not verified)
ext.document_type: Research paper, 8 pages, Springer LNCS-style layout (venue and year not visible). Metadata hint corrected: the third author is Harsh Vijay; the hint's author list is shortened.
ext.coverage: Read the full extracted text (410 lines, about 18k chars) in one pass: front matter, abstract, Sections 1-6, both data sections, Tables 1-2, figure captions, and references. Nothing skipped. Topics touched: social search and path-finding, influence and tie strength in networks. Not present: lobbying, elections, legislators, persuasion/turnout, allocation, text measurement. Annotation file read in full: 42 Highlight items by Paul Goff on pages 1-8, all with empty note text, so there are no sticky-note comments. Highlight colors are not interpreted.
ext.research_question: Does using directed, weighted influence edges (capturing asymmetry and tie strength) make social-search paths from source to target more effective than the hop-count shortest path given by Dijkstra? (Sec. 1, p.1-2; Abstract)
ext.theory: Influence of X on Y is the proportion of X's investment (interaction effort, time or count) directed at Y, normalized over all of X's investments; influence is asymmetric and lies between 0 and 1 (Sec. 3.1-3.3, p.3-4, citing Hangal et al. 2010 [5]). Tie strength from Granovetter's weak-ties argument motivates the weighting (Sec. 1.1, p.2). Global social search is treated as routing along the most influential path (Sec. 3, p.3).
ext.data: Two datasets. (1) DBLP subset: about 38,942 unique author names and 16 data-mining conferences, January 2001 to February 2010; nodes are authors; undirected co-authorship edges weighted by co-authored papers (Sec. 5.1, p.6). (2) Twitter: 15 days of crawled tweets, about 23,491 unique users and 32,132 directed retweet edges; undated (Sec. 5.2, p.6). Experimental unit: 500 randomly selected source-destination pairs per dataset (Sec. 5.1, p.6). The Table 1 caption says "500 total nodes in the network", which conflicts with the stated network sizes; this is read here as the pair count, since the Table 1 counts sum to 500 per dataset.
ext.method: Descriptive comparison of two path algorithms on the same source-destination pairs. Baseline: Dijkstra shortest path, measured by hop count, ties broken at random (Sec. 4, p.5; Sec. 5.1). Comparator: influence-based strongest path (Algorithm 1, from [5]), which enumerates candidate paths, multiplies edge influences along each path, and returns the path minimizing log(1/D) + log(1/product of influences) with D = 0.95 (p.5). Edge influence: DBLP = Papers(vi,vj)/sum_k Papers(vj,vk) (Eq. 2, p.6); Twitter = Retweets(Y,X)/sum_Z Retweets(Y,Z) (Eq. 3, p.6); general form Eq. 1 (p.4). Outcome measures: path length in hops and mean influence. No significance tests.
ext.identification: None. No causal design, no randomized or quasi-experimental variation. The two algorithms are compared descriptively on the same sampled pairs.
ext.scope: Population: DBLP authors in 16 selected data-mining conferences (2001-2010) and Twitter users in a 15-day undated window. Institutions: none studied. Era: 2001-2010 DBLP data; Twitter window undated. Generalization is claimed to "social networks" and "online social networks" (Abstract; Sec. 6) from two datasets only.

key_findings.finding: Influence is asymmetric; most node-level influence values lie below one. DBLP influence is more evenly distributed, while highly influential Twitter nodes sit in the tail of the distribution.
Twitter: the shortest path was smaller than the strongest path in most pairs; the two were equal in the rest.
DBLP: the strongest path was longer than the shortest in fewer pairs, and equal in a majority.

Average path lengths: strongest paths are longer by about 1.9 hops (Twitter) and 1.4 hops (DBLP) on average. The text says one or two hops (Twitter) and one hop (DBLP), which is looser than these means.
key_findings.numbers: Twitter: Avg |Pstrong| 6.8, Avg |Pshort| 4.9; DBLP: Avg |Pstrong| 4.7, Avg |Pshort| 3.3

key_findings.finding: The paper concludes that weighted influence search beats unweighted search and that influential paths beat random shortest paths. No path-quality or path-influence metric is reported, so 'better result' is asserted, not measured.
key_findings.location: Abstract p.1; Sec. 5.3 p.7; Sec. 6 Conclusion p.8

limitations: No limitations section. The paper says only that DBLP and Twitter differ because of structural differences (Sec. 5.3, p.7).
'Better result' and 'it is proved' (Abstract; Sec. 6) rest on path-length comparisons over a 500-pair sample; no path-quality metric and no statistical tests.
Two datasets only: a 2001-2010 data-mining subset of DBLP and a 15-day Twitter window; generalization is untested.
Influence definitions are narrow: DBLP uses co-authored papers in 16 conferences, Twitter uses retweets only.
Shortest-path ties are broken at random, so the equal/unequal shares depend on that choice (Sec. 5.1, p.6).
The 500-pair sample size is not justified by a power or convergence analysis; the Table 1 caption conflicts with the network sizes.

Algorithm 1 enumerates all simple paths (exponential; scale not discussed). The decay constant D = 0.95 is unjustified. Algorithm 2 (Dijkstra) pseudocode appears to push the unextended path and to use edge cost, while experiments count hops, so the baseline as coded is ambiguous.
Figure 1 is an illustrative four-node example (supervisor X and students A, B, Y; seven co-authored papers for A-X), not evidence.
measures: Path length in hops (Dijkstra and strongest path)
Total influence score log(1/D) + log(1/product of edge influences), D = 0.95
Share of pairs where strongest path length > shortest path length (Table 1)

rel.summary_md:
Ahmad, Ahmad and Vijay compare two ways of finding a social-search path between a source and a target. The first is plain Dijkstra, measured in hops. The second is the "strongest path" of Hangal et al. (2010). In that method, each directed edge carries an influence weight: the share of one node's total interaction investment that goes to the other node. The method then picks the path that minimises log(1/D) plus the log of 1 over the product of edge influences, with D = 0.95. The test uses 500 random source-target pairs in each of two networks: a DBLP co-authorship subset (2001-2010, about 38.9k authors) and a 15-day Twitter retweet graph (about 23.5k users, 32k directed edges). The strongest path was longer than the shortest in 64.6% of Twitter pairs and 45.0% of DBLP pairs. Mean lengths were 6.8 vs 4.9 hops on Twitter and 4.7 vs 3.3 on DBLP. The paper calls the weighted search "better", but it reports no measure of path quality, no outcome and no significance test. What it actually shows is only that the weighted route differs from the hop route and is longer. It is a method note, not evidence about legislatures.

For Paul's systems, it matters in three places:
- **Staffer closeness router.** Its hop cost, -ln(0.8 x strength), has the same form as Hangal's per-hop log(1/D) + log(1/influence), with D = 0.8 instead of 0.95. So this paper is a method source for that router, but it gives no validation of it.
- **Social interaction layer.** Its edge probability (events divided by the author's posting volume) is essentially the paper's Eq. 3 retweet influence. The layer then averages the two directions, which throws away the asymmetry the paper argues for.
- **Dashboard recruitment path.** The path matrix PE is directed, because receiver edge multipliers and role priors make it so. But the backward Dijkstra (distToTarget) multiplies edges in the forward direction away from the target. So the chain labelled "PROVABLY-OPTIMAL" is exactly max-product only when PE is symmetric. This is UNVERIFIED (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Strongest path minimizes log(1/D) + log(1/product of edge influences), D = 0.95 (Algorithm 1, from Hangal et al. 2010). Reported result: strongest paths are on average about 1.4 (DBLP) to 1.9 (Twitter) hops longer than shortest paths (Table 2: 4.7 vs 3.3; 6.8 vs 4.9). No path-quality metric is given.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 4, p.5 (Algorithm 1); Sec. 5.3 and Table 2, p.7
bearings.system_side: Hop cost = -ln(HOP_FACTOR x strength) + w x uncertainty, with HOP_FACTOR = 0.8. That equals ln(1/0.8) + ln(1/strength), the same per-hop decay-plus-log-inverse-weight form, solved exactly by bidirectional Dijkstra (heuristic 0) rather than by enumerating paths. Edges are undirected (one shared strength per pair).
bearings.transfer_conditions: Carries over only as a functional form: the router uses the Hangal-style objective. Carries no validity, because the paper never measures whether strongest paths succeed more often. Its decay constant (0.95) is as unjustified as the router's 0.8. The paper's influence is directed and normalized by the node's total investment; staffer strength is symmetric exposure, not a share of investment. The route cost is a heuristic model output, not an introduction probability (D-025).

bearings.paper_claim: Influence is asymmetric: high influence of X on Y does not imply the reverse, so edges must be directed (Sec. 3.3, p.3-4; Eq. 1-3). Mean node influence is 0.67 on Twitter and 0.60 on DBLP, and most values lie below 1 (Sec. 5.3, p.6-7).
bearings.system_side: The path matrix PE is directed. ADJ is symmetric, but PEBASE multiplies by the receiver's EMU[v], and PE then applies source_shock(u)/target_resistance(v). distToTarget(t) propagates d[v] = d[u] x PE[u][v] outward from the target, so dT[v] is the reliability of the chain t -> v. tracePath then scores the sponsor -> target direction with PE[cur][v] x dT[v]. When PE is asymmetric, the chain the code labels 'PROVABLY-OPTIMAL' max-product is therefore not exactly max-product in the sponsor-to-target direction. UNVERIFIED single-path reading (DE-062).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's general point about asymmetry is enough to show that edge direction matters for path search. The defect itself comes from reading the code, not from the paper. How large it is depends on how far EMU (0.80-1.20) and the role priors move PE[u][v] away from PE[v][u]. It may be small. A second path should confirm it (DE-062), for example by comparing against Dijkstra on the transposed PE.

bearings.paper_claim: Twitter influence(X,Y) = Retweets(Y,X) / sum_Z Retweets(Y,Z): a directed weight normalized by the actor's total retweet volume. Its asymmetry is the stated reason to use directed edges (Eq. 3, p.6; Sec. 3.3).
bearings.system_side: p(a->b) = weighted events(a->b) / max(25, posts(a)), capped at 0.25. This is the same per-author volume normalization as Eq. 3. The pair probability is then the MEAN of the two directions, and only a 'symmetric' edge list is emitted, so the direction the paper treats as the signal is discarded.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's evidence is descriptive: a 15-day undated Twitter crawl in which strongest paths are longer, with no outcome. It does not show that directed retweet edges predict anything legislative. It does give weak support for keeping a directed variant of this layer alongside the symmetric one before path or recruitment use. Per-edge volume normalization was REJECTED in this project's SNA tests; nothing here should be read as recommending wider volume normalization.

bearings.paper_claim: Tie-strength-weighted search should use a multiplicative product of normalized influences. Hop-count shortest paths ignore tie strength (Granovetter motivation, Sec. 1.1).
bearings.system_side: Overlap routes minimize the sum of ceil(1e6 x 128 / strength) plus one unit per introduction, with strength = proximity x log2(1 + days/30). Costs are additive inverse strengths, not -log of a bounded weight, so they cannot be read as a product of per-hop reliabilities.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Context only. The paper does not compare inverse-strength costs with log-product costs, and the overlap router is a deliberate design choice. Shared work days are a heuristic tie measure, not a measure of access or influence (D-025). Influence language is barred on revolving-door edges.

gaps_exposed: The recruitment path's backward Dijkstra does not transpose a directed PE. Nothing checks that the 'provably optimal' chain is optimal when receiver and role multipliers make edges asymmetric (UNVERIFIED; needs a second path).
The social interaction layer computes directed probabilities but publishes only their mean. No directed social edge reaches path search or recruitment.

No router (member recruitment, staffer closeness or staffer overlap) has an outcome log against which 'strongest' and 'shortest' routes could be compared. The paper never measured this either, so the strongest-vs-shortest question stays open in both.
flags: The paper's influence weight (an edge divided by the actor's total investment) is a volume normalization. Per-edge volume normalization was measured and REJECTED in this project's SNA tests: cite the paper as a method description only, never as grounds to extend volume normalization to the cosponsor or staffer graphs.

The paper's claims that 'it is proved' and 'better result' (Abstract; Sec. 6) rest only on path-length differences over 500 pairs, with no outcome or test. Do not quote them as validation of any router.

The Table 1 caption says '500 total nodes in the network', which conflicts with the stated network sizes; read it as 500 pairs. Any figure quoted from the paper must name the window (DBLP 2001-2010; Twitter 15 days, undated) and the denominator (500 pairs).
The dashboard-path asymmetry finding is new agent analysis and stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
Route costs and strengths are heuristic model outputs, not introduction or access probabilities (D-025).
rel.paul_alignment: Paul's highlights centre on the asymmetric definition of influence, the comparison between Dijkstra and the strongest path, and the conclusion that weighted search beats unweighted search. He left no notes, and his positions list Ahmad only under member-recruitment-path, as the strongest-path citation. The system partly matches that reading. The staffer closeness router uses the Hangal objective form, with D = 0.8. The recruitment path uses a most-reliable (max-product) Dijkstra, which follows Chen 2016 more closely than Ahmad. Where the system departs from the asymmetry Paul highlighted: the social layer averages away direction, and the recruitment path's backward pass does not respect PE's direction. Paul's highlighted line about "better result" goes further than the evidence, since the paper measures only path length. His takeaway should be held as a method preference, not as a validated finding.

related.why: Same objective (maximize the product of edge probabilities, i.e. Dijkstra on -log p). The dashboard recruitment path cites Chen for exactly the form Ahmad and Hangal call the strongest path.
Both draw on Granovetter's tie strength and stress directionality; Paul cites Haythornthwaite for directed ties in the same pathfinding and SNA components.
Directed single-source shortest paths. That fast-SSSP line of work is what an exact strongest-path search would use in place of Ahmad's exponential path enumeration.
Covers heuristic (A*-family) pathfinding variants of the Dijkstra baseline compared here; both are cited for member-recruitment-path.
Discusses retweet and mention data as relational evidence, which is the Twitter influence definition (Eq. 3) used here.
